quiz.q: In steady level flight, lift equals…
quiz.why: Vertical forces balance.

quiz.q: The Wright Flyer first flew in…
quiz.why: December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk.

quiz.q: A trade study…
quiz.why: It ranks options systematically.

quiz.q: The first step of the design process is…
quiz.why: Requirements drive everything after.

quiz.q: Engineers design the aircraft first and then find a mission for it.
quiz.why: The mission and its requirements come first.

quiz.q: In level flight thrust must balance weight.
quiz.why: Thrust balances drag; lift balances weight.

quiz.q: Shaving a little weight saves only that weight.
quiz.why: Weight savings compound through wing size, drag and fuel.

quiz.q: A 1,100 kg light airplane cruises level. How much lift must its wing produce? Give your answer in N.
The Wright Flyer’s first flight covered 36 m in 12 s. What was its average ground speed? Give your answer in m/s.
quiz.why: 3 m/s over the ground. It flew into a strong headwind, so its airspeed was much higher.

quiz.q: An airliner of mass 70,000 kg cruises level. Find its lift. Give your answer in N.
In level cruise an aircraft’s engines give 30 kN of thrust. What is its drag?
quiz.why: 30 kN, since thrust balances drag in steady flight.

quiz.q: Published lift data were unreliable, so they measured many wing shapes themselves: testing before building is the heart of the design process.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. Why did the Wright brothers build a wind tunnel?

quiz.q: A tie at 7.2: the team should test both or revisit the weights it trusts least.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. Two wing concepts are scored out of 10 on cost (weight 0.3), efficiency (0.5) and ease of building (0.2). Concept A scores 8, 6, 9; B scores 5, 9, 6. Which wins?

quiz.q: Design priorities change with the times. Requirements for new aircraft now include fuel burn and emissions, so the same trade-study tools weigh climate alongside cost and performance.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: NASA lists three main ways to make aviation sustainable: efficient aircraft technology, sustainable aviation fuel, and better operations and infrastructure.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: On December 17, 1903, the Wright Flyer made a 12-second flight covering 36 m (120 ft); the best flight that day covered 260 m (852 ft) in 59 seconds. The Wrights succeeded by testing: they built gliders and their own wind tunnel before adding an engine.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Every design starts with a mission: payload, range or orbit, cost, safety. Requirements turn the mission into numbers the design must meet.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Design is iterative: concept sketch, sizing, analysis, test, redesign. A trade study compares options against weighted criteria.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Four forces act on an aircraft: lift, weight, thrust and drag. In steady level flight, lift = weight and thrust = drag.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Weight compounds: extra structure needs more lift, a bigger wing, more drag, more fuel, and more weight again.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.
